newsitem.title: UK: London aims to corner post-EMU money market rates.
newsitem.headline: London aims to corner post-EMU money market rates.

text.p: London can dominate money market dealings in the euro from the start of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999, even though sterling is likely to be out of the system, financial experts here said.

The British Bankers' Association (BBA) and the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) are working to develop a daily fixing for money market rates based on the euro, known as euro Libor.

Britain's banking professional body and its main futures exchange hope financial contracts currently based on industry standard Libor (London interbank offered rate) will move seamlessly to the new rate.
"The big majority of all the swap, money and FRA (forward rate agreement) markets use Libor," said Guiliano Gregorio, LIFFE's director of business development for interest rate products.

LIFFE has changed the contract specifications of its Euromark, short sterling, Eurolira and Ecu futures and options contracts to allow for the replacement of the existing BBA-fixed Libor rate by a euro Libor rate post-EMU.
"The reference rate will be a Libor rate, preferably the BBA rate," said Gregorio.

Britain, by many accounts, has the economic muscle but lacks the political will to join a single currency in 1999. The country goes to the polls on May 1, and both leading British political parties have said an early EMU entry is unlikely.
But London claims its supremacy in money markets will hold sway even in an EMU world from which it is excluded.
"It doesn't make any difference," said Gregorio. "It is the Libor rate at which all the Euromarks are settled."
The German futures exchange, the DTB, has rejected its home-grown money market reference rate, Fibor, in favour of Libor.
Bob Blower, assistant director at the BBA, said exclusion from EMU would not affect London's ability to hold on to its money market business. He cited Eurodollars as an example.
"We are not part of the United States, yet the CME (Chicago Mercantile Exchange) has started to price its Eurodollar contract against Libor," Blower said.

London accounts for 22 percent of global banking assets, and over a third of all foreign exchange business is done in London, he said. "The liquidity is certainly here, and we expect that to continue."
The Libor fixing for a range of currencies is based on rates supplied by 16 banks. All the banks must have a London office, and need to be active in cash as well as derivatives markets.
But continental bankers would like to see a central euro fixing, based on rates provided from banks in different cities.
There could be room for both kinds of fixing, some industry officials said.

"If Libor is going to be your cost of funds because you match funding, then you want a rate in one city, because you only borrow in one city," said Clifford Dammers, secretary general of the International Primary Market Association (IPMA), at a recent conference on EMU.
"If you are using it as an index for pricing deals, then maybe a pan-European rate is appropriate."
Banks may also continue post-EMU to quote rates in individual EMU currencies, to cope with outstanding instruments, such as floating rate notes, which rely on a regular Libor fixing.
But Dammers was doubtful this would be necessary.
"I do not see any need to quote franc or mark Libor rates, so long as the central banks stand ready to convert the euro in and out at no charge," said Dammers.
